# Every covolume-pi lattice occurs: a classical existence proof

Snapshot: 2026-10-14 (America/Los_Angeles).

## Claim and evidence boundary

**Theorem U.** For every full-rank lattice `Lambda` in the oriented Euclidean plane with covolume `pi`, there is an irrational badly approximable `alpha in (0,1)` such that, for every rotation `S in SO(2)` and every `b in R^2`, `S Lambda+b` is a Chabauty–Fell limit of translates of

`X_alpha = {sqrt(n) exp(2*pi*i*n*alpha) : n=1,2,...}`

by translation vectors whose norms tend to infinity. The same `alpha` works for all these rotations and translates of the chosen lattice. It may depend on the lattice's shape. The translations contain **no rotations or dilations**.

This is the exact universal-existence question in Tevet's September 2025 preprint, Further Questions p. 12, strengthened only by spelling out rotation/translation freedom. It is not the full elastic-energy or chirality conjecture in Cao's book chapter. The older Fermat-tail density law is not claimed as a discovery.

**Verdict: SOLVED for Theorem U. Evidence label: Certification (written classical proof). FRONTIER_METHOD: DELIVERY-READY for external mathematical scrutiny; NOVELTY-UNCLEAR for worldwide priority.** The finite smoke passed; the completed Claude referee returned **CORRECT**, and Codex returned **CORRECT-WITH-FIXES**, finding no theorem gap and two minor finite-evidence scope issues. Their findings and author dispositions are recorded in §9. Neither model agreement nor the finite smoke is a formal-kernel or priority certificate.

## 1. Definitions and exact imported result

Write `Bad` for the set of real irrational numbers `x` for which there is `c>0` such that `|x-p/q| >= c/q^2` for all integers `p` and `q>=1`, as in McMullen. Tevet instead defines bad approximability by `liminf_j q_j*|q_j*x-p_j|>0` over convergents, and states its bounded-digit characterization in §4, p. 6. The elementary bridge below verifies both conventions for every number used here; it does not silently identify differently stated definitions. Integer translation and negation preserve the uniform definition directly.

The non-elementary imported input is **McMullen's absolute-winning theorem**, with its exact accompanying invariances:

1. For a hyperbolic lattice `Gamma` with a cusp at infinity, the set `D(Gamma)` of endpoints of bounded projected geodesic rays is absolutely winning. For `Gamma=SL_2(Z)`, this set is exactly `Bad`. This is Theorem 1.3 and the preceding identification, author manuscript p. 3.
2. An absolute-winning subset of `R^n` remains absolute winning under any global quasisymmetric homeomorphism of `R^n`. This is Theorem 2.2, manuscript p. 5.
3. Countable intersections of absolute-winning sets are absolute winning: §1, “Absolute winning,” property (2), p. 3. Only an intersection of two sets is needed here, and a direct proof below addresses the possibly nonshrinking-radius game convention. Such a set meets every nonempty open interval because Bob may choose his initial closed interval inside it and the winning intersection lies in that initial interval.

Primary source: Curtis T. McMullen, *Winning sets, quasiconformal maps and Diophantine approximation*, author manuscript dated 11 August 2009; published in *Geometric and Functional Analysis* (2010), DOI [10.1007/s00039-010-0078-3](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-010-0078-3). [Author PDF](https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/papers/home/text/papers/winning/winning.pdf), pinned locally as `source/mcmullen-winning.pdf`.

The proof does **not** import a claim that a generic dense geodesic is bounded, a symbolic-dynamics specification theorem, or Tevet's shortest-neighbor Proposition 8. It does not infer local density from global Hausdorff dimension alone.

**Elementary bad-approximability bridge.** For any irrational `y` with simple-CF digits `d_i` and convergents `P_j/Q_j`, the complete-quotient identity derived in §3, with the sign removed, gives

`Q_j*|Q_j*y-P_j|=1/(d_(j+1)+eta_j+Q_(j-1)/Q_j)`, `0<eta_j<1`.

If `y in Bad` with uniform constant `c`, the left side is at least `c`, so `d_(j+1)<1/c`. Thus the selected ratios have bounded positive digits. Conversely, digits bounded by `M` give `Q_j*|Q_j*y-P_j|>=1/(M+2)`, hence Tevet's positive-liminf condition. They also give the uniform condition without importing a best-approximation theorem: for any `p` and `q>=1`, choose the first convergent denominator `Q_j>=2q`. The recurrence gives `Q_j<2(M+1)q`, and the same complete-quotient identity gives `|Q_j*y-P_j|<1/Q_(j+1)<=1/(2q)`. The integer `p*Q_j-q*P_j` is nonzero, since the reduced denominator `Q_j` exceeds `q`. Therefore

`1 <= |p*Q_j-q*P_j| <= Q_j*|q*y-p|+q*|Q_j*y-P_j|`

implies `|y-p/q|>1/(4(M+1)q^2)`. Both required definitions are satisfied by the constructed angle.

**Finite absolute-winning intersection, including radius decay.** Fix a game parameter `0<delta<1/3`. To intersect two absolute-winning sets, play the first set's `delta^3` strategy in rounds `1,4,7,...`, the second's in rounds `2,5,8,...`, and remove a centered interval of length `delta*|B_i|` in rounds `3,6,9,...`. The strategy moves have size at most `delta^3*|B_i|<=delta*|B_i|`. Consecutive Bob intervals in either subgame have length ratio at least `delta^3` and avoid that subgame's previous deletion, so both subgames are legal. Each centered deletion forces the next Bob interval into one side of length at most `(1-delta)*|B_i|/2`; such a legal move exists because `delta<1/3`. Thus all radii tend to zero. Both subgame intersections are the same single point, lying in both winning sets. This proves the finite-intersection fact actually used, while global bi-Lipschitz transport remains a directly applicable case of the explicitly cited Theorem 2.2.

## 2. Put an arbitrary lattice into two badly approximable ratios

Identify the plane with `C`. Choose any negatively oriented basis `V,W0` of `Lambda`, so `det(V,W0)=-pi`. Adding an integer multiple of `V` to `W0` changes neither the lattice nor the determinant. Choose that integer large enough that the resulting basis `V,W` satisfies

`W/V = x-i*h`, with `x>1`, `h>0`.

Indeed `h=pi/|V|^2`. For a real parameter

`h/(x+1) < t < h/x`,

put `A=|V|/sqrt(1+t^2)`, `C=t*A`, and choose the rotation `R` of angle `arg(V)-arctan(t)`. Then

`R^(-1)V = A+i*C`,

`R^(-1)W = (x-i*h)(A+i*C) = A*(x+h*t) + i*A*(x*t-h)`.

Consequently

`R^(-1)V = (A,C)`,  `R^(-1)W = (A*beta,-C*u)`,

where

`beta=x+h*t > 1`,  `u=h/t-x in (0,1)`.

The admissible beta interval is the nonempty open interval

`J = (x+h^2/(x+1), x+h^2/x)`.

On it,

`u=g(beta)=h^2/(beta-x)-x`,  `g'(beta)=-h^2/(beta-x)^2`.

Choose a nondegenerate closed interval `[a0,b0]` strictly inside `J`. Extend `g` from this interval to the whole real line using its tangent line at `a0` to the left and its tangent line at `b0` to the right. The extension `G` is a decreasing `C^1` bijection, and everywhere

`0 < h^2/(b0-x)^2 <= |G'| <= h^2/(a0-x)^2 < infinity`.

Thus `G` and its inverse are globally bi-Lipschitz, hence quasisymmetric. McMullen's results imply that

`Bad intersect G^(-1)(Bad)`

is absolute winning and therefore meets `(a0,b0)`. Choose `beta` in that intersection and set `u=g(beta)`. Both numbers are badly approximable, while every strict geometric inequality remains valid. Orientation reversal is allowed by McMullen's metric definition of quasisymmetry; alternatively apply the theorem to `-G`, since `-Bad=Bad`.

Finally the determinant gives the exact identity

`pi = A*C*(beta+u)`.                                                   (1)

This proves the required geometric lemma for **every** target lattice, including highly elongated and nonalgebraic ones. No computability assumption on the entries of its basis was used. The winning-set selection is an existence argument, not an advertised finite algorithm for arbitrary real input.

## 3. One bounded continued fraction realizes the two ratios

Set `a=floor(beta)` and `r=beta-a`. The inequality `beta>1` gives `a>=1`, while irrationality gives `0<r<1`; both `r` and `u` are badly approximable. Write

`r=[0;r1,r2,...]`,  `u=[0;u1,u2,...]`.

There is a finite integer `M` bounding `a`, `1`, every `ri` and every `ui`.

Construct one infinite digit word as follows. Starting with an empty prefix, at stage `k>=1`, let `ell` be the length already written. Choose `epsilon_k in {0,1}` so that `ell+epsilon_k+k` is even. Append `epsilon_k` copies of the digit **1**, then the block

`r_k,r_(k-1),...,r_1, a, u_1,u_2,...,u_k`.                             (2)

Let `j_k=ell+epsilon_k+k`, the position immediately before the central digit `a`. Thus `j_k` is even and the central digit has position `j_k+1`. The padding is **before** the prescribed block, so it does not damage either local digit window.

Let `alpha=[0;d1,d2,...]` be the number represented by the resulting infinite word. Every digit lies in `{1,...,M}`, so `alpha` is irrational and badly approximable. This is one fixed number, not a new number at each stage, and the bound `M` does not increase with `k`.

Use convergents `p_j/q_j=[0;d1,...,dj]`, with `p_-1=1,p_0=0,q_-1=0,q_0=1`. Define

`r_j=q_(j-1)/q_j=[0;d_j,d_(j-1),...,d_1]`,

`u_j=[0;d_(j+2),d_(j+3),...]`.

At `j=j_k`, these have initial digit strings `r1,...,rk` and `u1,...,uk`, respectively. To check convergence without invoking a coding theorem, recall the elementary cylinder formula. If `P_l/Q_l` are the convergents of `[0;e1,...,el]`, all continuations are

`(P_l+eta*P_(l-1))/(Q_l+eta*Q_(l-1))`,  `0<=eta<=1`.

The endpoint difference is

`1/(Q_l*(Q_l+Q_(l-1))) <= 1/Q_l^2`,

because `|P_l*Q_(l-1)-P_(l-1)*Q_l|=1`, obtained immediately from the convergent recurrence. Positive digits make `Q_l` grow at least as Fibonacci denominators. Therefore, along the specified even indices,

`r_j -> r`,  `u_j -> u`,  `q_(j+1)/q_j=a+r_j -> beta`.                 (3)

For completeness, the complete quotient at position `j+1` is `a+u_j`, so

`alpha=(p_j*(a+u_j)+p_(j-1))/(q_j*(a+u_j)+q_(j-1))`.

Subtract `p_j/q_j`, use the determinant recurrence, and use even `j` to get

`c_j=q_j*(q_j*alpha-p_j)=1/(a+u_j+r_j) -> c=1/(beta+u)`,                (4)

`q_(j+1)*alpha-p_(j+1)=-u_j*(q_j*alpha-p_j)`.                          (5)

The signs and parity in (4)–(5) are essential; they are not recovered from squared quantities.

## 4. The exact local lattices approach the chosen basis

For a positive integer `n`, let `rho=sqrt(n)` and define the full lattice

`L_n(alpha) = {(q/(2*rho), 2*pi*rho*(q*alpha-p)) : (q,p) in Z^2}`.     (6)

Its covolume is exactly `pi`. For the even index `j=j_k`, the integer pairs `(q_j,p_j)` and `(q_(j+1),p_(j+1))` have determinant `+1`. Hence they form an **entire basis**, not merely two independent vectors in a possible sublattice, of the integer input lattice in (6).

Choose `n_k` to be a nearest positive integer to `(q_j/(2*A))^2`, discarding finitely many early terms if necessary. Then `n_k -> infinity` and

`q_j/(2*sqrt(n_k)) -> A`.

In the basis above, `L_(n_k)` has matrix

`B_k = [[q_j/(2*sqrt(n_k)), q_(j+1)/(2*sqrt(n_k))],`
`       [2*pi*sqrt(n_k)*(q_j*alpha-p_j),`
`        2*pi*sqrt(n_k)*(q_(j+1)*alpha-p_(j+1))]]`.

Equations (3)–(5) and (1) yield

`B_k -> B = [[A,A*beta],[C,-C*u]]`,  `det(B)=-pi`.                     (7)

Indeed the first lower entry tends to `pi*c/A=C`, and the second tends to `-C*u`. This proves an actual limit to the chosen lattice coordinates, not just a dense approximation among different angles.

Convergence of nonsingular basis matrices implies local convergence of their lattices: every `B*z`, `z in Z^2`, is approximated by `B_k*z`; conversely, bounded `B_k*z_k` have bounded integer `z_k` since the inverses `B_k^(-1)` are uniformly bounded, so every convergent subsequence has a further subsequence with constant `z_k`. Thus `L_(n_k) -> B Z^2` in the Chabauty–Fell topology.

Here and below the local sequential criterion implies the precise metric topology used by Tevet. For closed sets `F_k,F`, suppose every point of `F` is approached by points of `F_k`, and every convergent subsequence of bounded points from `F_k` limits into `F`. If points in `F_k` inside a fixed closed ball stayed at distance at least `epsilon` from `F`, compactness would produce a limiting point contradicting the second condition. Conversely, cover the compact set `F` in that ball by finitely many `epsilon/3`-balls centered in `F`; the first condition approximates their centers simultaneously for all sufficiently large `k`. These give both neighborhood inclusions on the ball of radius `1/epsilon`, and hence Tevet's `Delta -> 0`. This also justifies the subsequent transfers using (8)–(9).

## 5. Uniform local comparison with the actual spiral

Local lattice linearization and covolume `pi` are prior art: Roland Bacher, “On geodesics of phyllotaxis,” *Confluentes Mathematici* **6**(1), 3–27 (2014), [DOI/full text](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/cml.10.pdf), Theorem 1.1, Proposition 3.1, Corollary 3.2 and Remark 3.3. The explicit elementary bounds below were independently developed with the companion classification worker and are written out so the proof and reviews remain self-contained; no novelty is claimed for linearization itself. No companion implementation is imported or copied.

Let `P_n=sqrt(n)*exp(2*pi*i*n*alpha)`, `rho=sqrt(n)` and

`Y_n=exp(-2*pi*i*n*alpha)*(X_alpha-P_n)`.

The rotation in this definition is an **analysis coordinate frame**, not an allowed transformation of the spiral in the theorem.

**Forward bound.** Let `v=(q/(2*rho),2*pi*rho*(q*alpha-p)) in L_n` have norm at most `R`, and suppose `rho>=4*R`. Then `n+q>=n/2>0`, so the corresponding index is allowed. With `theta=2*pi*(q*alpha-p)` and `s=sqrt(n+q)`,

`Ypoint=s*exp(i*theta)-rho`,  `v=q/(2*rho)+i*rho*theta`.

Here `|q|<=2*R*rho`, `|theta|<=R/rho`, `s<=3*rho/2`, and

`|s-rho|<=2*R`,

`|s-rho-q/(2*rho)|=q^2/(2*rho*(s+rho)^2)<=2*R^2/rho`.

Using `|exp(i*theta)-1-i*theta|<=theta^2/2`,

`|Ypoint-v| <= 2*R^2/rho + 2*R^2/rho + 3*R^2/(4*rho)`
`             <= 5*R^2/rho`.                                         (8)

Also `|q*alpha-p|<=1/(8*pi)<1/2`, so `p` is the unique nearest integer to `q*alpha` in this local range.

**Reverse bound.** If `Ypoint=s*exp(i*theta)-rho` has norm at most `R` and `rho>=12*R`, choose the principal argument `theta=arg(rho+Ypoint)` and the integer `p` with `theta=2*pi*(q*alpha-p)`. Since `|s-rho|<=R`,

`|q/(2*rho)|<=R+R^2/(2*rho)<=25*R/24`.

The real part of `rho+Ypoint` is positive, and

`|theta|<=R/(rho-R)`, hence `|rho*theta|<=12*R/11`.

Thus the corresponding `v` has norm less than `3*R`. Apply (8) at radius `3*R` to obtain

`|Ypoint-v|<=45*R^2/rho`.                                             (9)

These are neighborhood inclusions into the **full** opposing sets. They are not an incorrect same-radius truncated Hausdorff claim, which would be sensitive to points on the ball boundary. For each fixed `R`, the errors tend to zero. Equations (8)–(9) and the basis convergence in (7) therefore imply `Y_(n_k) -> B Z^2`.

## 6. Physical orientation without rotating any translate

For any positive integers `m,n`, the model lattices obey the exact relation

`L_m = diag(sqrt(n/m),sqrt(m/n))*L_n`.                                 (10)

Thus changing `n_k` by an integer `b_k` with `b_k=o(n_k)` does not alter the limit in (7).

We need the following elementary uniform form of irrational-rotation density. For an irrational `alpha` and any `epsilon>0`, some finite set `{exp(2*pi*i*b*alpha):0<=b<=H}` is an epsilon-net of the unit circle. One proof uses pigeonhole to find `0<||q*alpha||<delta`, then uses the points at indices `0,q,2q,...,floor(1/||q*alpha||)*q`; they traverse a circle grid in one of the two directions with gaps at most `||q*alpha||`. Take `delta` arbitrarily small. Rotating this finite net by any starting phase preserves the net property.

Let `H_k=floor(sqrt(n_k))`. Then `H_k -> infinity` and `H_k/n_k -> 0`. For any desired rotation `R_theta`, choose `0<=b_k<=H_k` so that

`exp(2*pi*i*(n_k+b_k)*alpha) -> exp(i*theta)`.

The finite-net argument gives this for the whole sequence, not only a subsequence; for example choose a distance-minimizing index in each finite window. Set `m_k=n_k+b_k`. Equation (10) preserves the model-lattice limit, and the local comparison applies equally at `m_k`. Therefore

`X_alpha-P_(m_k) -> R_theta*B Z^2`.                                   (11)

Explicitly, writing `omega_k=exp(2*pi*i*m_k*alpha)`, one has `X_alpha-P_(m_k)=omega_k*Y_(m_k)`. Rotations preserve origin-centered balls, and on a ball of radius `R` their additional error is at most `R*|omega_k-exp(i*theta)|`. Therefore the uniform local inclusions pass to the desired rotated limit. A fixed affine shift uses the same inclusions on a ball enlarged by `|b|`. These are continuity arguments for the limits; no rotation or dilation is inserted into the actual translating maps.

Take `R_theta=R` from §2 to obtain `Lambda`. Every other physical rotation is obtained by choosing another target angle, with the **same** `alpha`. Adding a fixed vector `b` to the translating maps gives `R_theta*B Z^2+b`, and

`|-P_(m_k)+b| >= sqrt(m_k)-|b| -> infinity`.

All transformations in (11) are translations. The coordinate rotation in §5 disappears through the selected phases; there is no post-hoc rotation or dilation. This completes the proof of Theorem U.

## 7. What was and was not settled

- **Settled by the written proof:** the full all-lattice existence statement with covolume exactly `pi`, a single fixed badly approximable angle for each shape, translation-only escape to infinity, and arbitrary orientation/affine offset.
- **Not asserted:** one badly approximable angle works for every lattice shape; an effective uniform bound on partial quotients independent of the target; a finite algorithm selecting the winning-set point for arbitrary noncomputable real input; optimal packing or elastic-energy selection; the book's cone chirality conjecture.
- **Why the core obligation is bounded:** two simultaneous badly-approximable real ratios are selected by a published winning-set theorem; an explicit bounded-alphabet block construction realizes them. No bounded-orbit realization or generic-geodesic assumption remains.
- **Novelty boundary:** the exact question is explicitly open in the cited 2025 preprint. A bounded follow-up screen cannot establish worldwide priority, and a classical proof assembled here is labeled Certification rather than automatically Discovery.

## 8. Frozen finite verification protocol

Inspect integer basis combinations in `[-2,2]^2` and phase windows of lengths `128,512,2048`. All numerical observations remain Empirical evidence even when accompanied by conservative cylinder bounds.

They exercise §§3–6, not the general `x>1` basis normalization or the nonconstructive selection in §2. The numerical midpoint is one fixed rational proxy inside the same infinite angle's exact cylinder; it is not itself asserted to be the infinite badly approximable angle.

# Spiral Delone sets with uniform asymptotic density

The physics-book chapter by Cao Zexian, *Are the Fibonacci Parastichous Spirals a Least-Energy Configuration on Conical Surface?* (Science Press, 2009, pp. 541–543), concerns the geometry of packing identical units and phyllotactic arrangements. The user-approved reselection here addresses a **different, precise mathematical subproblem suggested by that packing/phyllotaxis theme**, not the full elastic-energy or cone-packing conjecture.

## Exact target and eligibility

Adiceam and Tsokanos, *Higher Dimensional Spiral Delone Sets*, arXiv:2010.06428v3 (30 March 2021), §6, pp. 22–23, explicitly ask whether a spiral Delone set in ambient dimension `n>=3` can have asymptotic density. The required points are `s_k=k^(1/n)u_k`, `u_k` on the unit sphere, and the density limit is required for **every bounded Jordan-measurable set**, not only origin-centered balls. The normalization `1/V_n` was verified against both rendered source pages and the exact radial count. Later-source clearance is recorded separately in `STATUS.md`.

**Verdict: SOLVED for this precise existence theorem, in every fixed `n>=2` (hence all `n>=3`). Correctness state: DELIVERY-READY. Evidence label: Certification; novelty/priority remains uncertified.** Sort all nonzero integer lattice vectors `z_k` by Euclidean norm with lexicographic ties and set `s_k=k^(1/n) z_k/|z_k|`. The complete proof gives a vanishing displacement from `V_n^(1/n) Z^n \\ {0}`, uniformly through ties; global separation including finite/cross-prefix pairs; global covering; density `lambda_n(X)/V_n` for every bounded Jordan set; and angular uniform distribution. The classical lattice discrepancy and all bridges are written in `RESULTS.md`. The independent other-vendor referee found the argument correct, with four minor clarifications integrated. No full cone-energy solution, optimal packing claim, or first-in-literature claim is made.

## Contract and file map

- `source/problem.zh.txt`: unmodified book excerpt copied from the earlier cone intake.
- `source/adiceam-tsokanos-v3.pdf`, selected page images and `source/primary-evidence.json`: pinned public primary source and normalization/open-question evidence.
- `STATUS.md`: explicit primary open statement, later citing works, mathematical baseline, and limits of novelty screening.
- `RESULTS.md`: complete argument, precise hypotheses, evidence labels and independent-review dispositions.
- `code/verify.py`, `results/verification.json`: deterministic lattice construction and scientific boundary/negative controls; finite checks are not a Delone proof.
- `review/`: read-only independent referee prompt, untouched result and receipt.
- `review/source-audits.json`: separate forward-citation and classical/prior-construction audits, with access limitations.

## One-command scientific replay

From this directory:

```sh
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 /Users/jinleic/jinleic-workspace/scratch/ai4s-venv/bin/python code/verify.py
```

Observed: exit 0, **five PASS groups**, and `results/verification.json`. The deterministic 3D sample has 57,776 points; independent exact enumerators and tie/normalization/negative controls are included. These finite checks do not prove the universal statement or supply global separation/covering constants—the written proof does.

3. **Bessel formulas.** [NIST DLMF 10.9.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.9.E4) supplies the integral representation with \(\Re\nu>-1/2\); [DLMF 10.17.3](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.17.E3) supplies the fixed-order positive-real large-argument decay. 4. **No priority claim from a local proof.** Sorting a lattice and using its discrepancy are classical ingredients. The construction's historical status is a separate source question; an indexed-citation miss is not proof of worldwide novelty. Even if the construction answers the exact stated question, the evidence category may properly be **Certification**, not a new-method Discovery.
5. **Historical attribution and smoothing source.** The classical audit read the relevant portions of **Ivić–Krätzel–Kühleitner–Nowak**, “Lattice points in large regions and related arithmetic functions: Recent developments in a very classic topic,” [arXiv:math/0410522v1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410522), §3.2, pp.16–17, and **W. M. Schmidt**, “Edmund Hlawka (1916–2009),” *Acta Arithmetica* **139**(4) (2009), [10.4064/aa139-4-1](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa139-4-1). ## Earlier-construction check and remaining access limits

The separate classical audit read **Marklof**, “Delone sets generated by square roots,” [arXiv:2003.08319v1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.08319), all five pages: Proposition 1 gives the planar density/angular-distribution equivalence, and Proposition 3 gives a particular planar square-root-angle spiral. MathOverflow discussions [145963](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/145963), [146398](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/146398), and [302348](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/302348) were read by that audit. They concern increasing-radius lattice walks, lattice-free radial gaps and thin spherical shells, respectively. No exact-radius rank-rescaling solution to this target was located there; these are discussion sources, not refereed papers.

One unresolved older lead is **V. N. Berestovskii**, “Spiral dispositions of nonnegative integers at lattice points,” *Matematicheskie Trudy* **8**(2),49–68 (2005); English translation *Siberian Advances in Mathematics* **16**(2),43–61 (2006). 1	# Norm-ranked lattice spirals: proof and evidence
2	
3	**Verdict: SOLVED for the exact existence statement below in every fixed dimension \(n\ge2\), hence for every \(n\ge3\) asked about. Correctness state: DELIVERY-READY. Evidence: Certification, not a priority-certified Discovery.** A completed independent other-vendor referee found the proof correct; its minor clarifications and dispositions appear at the end. The broad physics-book cone-energy problem is not solved here.

5	
6	Date: 2026-10-14 (PT). **Evidence label: Certification of the written theorem below; novelty/priority is not established by this label.** The classical lattice-discrepancy argument is a reproduction of established Fourier/Poisson machinery. Finite computations are Empirical evidence or exact finite identity checks, not a substitute for the infinite-set argument. Independent review and the later-source screen are recorded separately.
7	
8	## 1. Exact obligation and frozen research contract
9	
10	The target is the explicit density question in Adiceam–Tsokanos, *Higher Dimensional Spiral Delone Sets*, arXiv:2010.06428v3, §6, pp. 22–23. Their points have **exact radii** \(k^{1/n}\), with arbitrary spherical directions. Their asymptotic-density limit is required for **every bounded measurable set whose boundary has zero Lebesgue measure**. Merely counting origin-centered balls does not answer the question.
11	
12	- **Claim:** the norm-ranked nonzero integer lattice construction below gives a Delone spiral with the required density and angular uniform distribution in every fixed dimension \(n\ge2\), hence in every dimension asked about, \(n\ge3\).
13	- **Baseline:** their paper constructs spiral Delone sets in every dimension but explicitly leaves the additional density/angular-equidistribution condition open. The classical smooth-ball lattice discrepancy is an ingredient, not a claimed new estimate.
14	- **Load-bearing bridge:** an error \(o(R^{n-1})\) in the lattice-ball count makes the radial rank correction \(o(1)\), including all points tied on a lattice sphere. A volume main term \(N(R)\sim V_nR^n\) alone does not supply that bridge.
15	- **Scope:** arbitrary directions are allowed by the source definition. No continuity, bounded step between consecutive indices, transitive-map orbit, distinctness of directions, or visually sunflower-like appearance is claimed. The points themselves are distinct because their radii are distinct. Every nonzero lattice vector is used, including nonprimitive vectors.
16	- **Book connection:** this is a higher-dimensional phyllotaxis/regular-packing subproblem, not a theorem about elastic energy, cone packing, Fibonacci optimality, or a minimum-energy configuration.
17	- **Frozen scientific controls:** two independent exact lattice enumerators, complete and partially cut tie shells, normalization and exponent identities, 3D ball Fourier-transform identity, and deterministic 3D geometric/density observations. Main geometric sample: all nonzero integer points in the ball of radius 24; smaller radii 4, 8, 12, 16 check prefix consistency. Directional counts and translated Jordan-box counts include negative controls. No optimizer, fitted parameter, or learned model is used. Single-thread numerical libraries; no giant search.
18	
19	## 2. The theorem
20	
21	Write
22	\[
23	V_n=\lambda_n(B_1)=\frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(1+n/2)},\qquad c_n=V_n^{1/n}.
24	\]
25	Enumerate \(\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) as \((z_k)_{k\ge1}\), in nondecreasing Euclidean norm, with lexicographic order within equal-norm shells. Put
26	\[
27	r_k=\|z_k\|_2,\qquad u_k=z_k/r_k,\qquad s_k=k^{1/n}u_k,\qquad S=\{s_k:k\ge1\}.
28	\tag{2.1}
29	\]
30	
31	**Theorem.** For each fixed integer \(n\ge2\):
32	
33	1. (2.1) is effectively constructible and \(\|s_k\|_2=k^{1/n}\) exactly.
34	2. With \(\beta_n=(n-1)/(n+1)>0\),
35	   \[
36	   \|s_k-c_nz_k\|_2=O_n(r_k^{-\beta_n})=o(1).
37	   \tag{2.2}
38	   \]
39	   The estimate is uniform over all ranks within any tied shell; the conclusion does not depend on the chosen order inside ties.
40	3. \(S\) is uniformly discrete and relatively dense in \(\mathbb R^n\), including the finite initial part.
41	4. For every bounded Jordan-measurable \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\),
42	   \[
43	   \lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{\#(S\cap RX)}{R^n}
44	   =\frac{\lambda_n(X)}{V_n}.
45	   \tag{2.3}
46	   \]
47	5. For every spherical cap \(C\subset\mathbb S^{n-1}\),
48	   \[
49	   \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\#\{1\le k\le N:u_k\in C\}}{N}
50	   =\frac{\sigma_{n-1}(C)}{\sigma_{n-1}(\mathbb S^{n-1})}.
51	   \tag{2.4}
52	   \]
53	
54	No numerical value of the global separation or covering constant is inferred from a finite nearest-neighbor computation. Their existence is proved in §5.
55	
56	## 3. Ball-count lemma, with a special-case proof
57	
58	Define the full closed-ball count
59	\[
60	N_0(R)=\#\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:\|z\|_2\le R\}.
61	\]
62	For all real \(R\ge2\), we prove
63	\[
64	N_0(R)=V_nR^n+O_n(R^{\alpha_n}),\qquad
65	\alpha_n=\frac{n(n-1)}{n+1}=n-2+\frac{2}{n+1}.
66	\tag{3.1}
67	\]
68	In particular \(\alpha_n<n-1\). The constant may depend on fixed dimension; no dimension-uniform constant is asserted.
69	
70	### 3.1 Fourier transform and its decay
71	
72	Use the Fourier convention
73	\(\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx\).
74	For \(\xi\ne0\), rotation invariance and slicing perpendicular to \(\xi\) give
75	\[
76	\widehat{1_{B_R}}(\xi)
77	=V_{n-1}\int_{-R}^{R}(R^2-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}
78	 e^{-2\pi i\|\xi\|t}\,dt
79	=R^{n/2}\|\xi\|^{-n/2}J_{n/2}(2\pi R\|\xi\|).
80	\tag{3.2}
81	\]
82	The last equality is Poisson's Bessel integral, [NIST DLMF 10.9.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.9.E4), with fixed real order \(\nu=n/2>-1/2\). The constants follow from \(V_{n-1}=\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)\); substituting \(t=Rv\) into the first integral makes (3.2) immediate from that identity.
83	
84	For fixed order, [DLMF 10.17.3](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.17.E3) gives
85	\(J_{n/2}(x)=O_n(x^{-1/2})\) as positive real \(x\to\infty\). Continuity on compact positive intervals extends the bound to all \(x\ge1\). Hence, when \(R\ge1\) and \(\|\xi\|\ge1\),
86	\[
87	|\widehat{1_{B_R}}(\xi)|
88	\le A_n R^{(n-1)/2}\|\xi\|^{-(n+1)/2}.
89	\tag{3.3}
90	\]
91	These are established special-function identities; neither the formula nor its decay is a new result here.
92	
93	For the requested ambient dimension three, no Bessel asymptotic is necessary: direct integration of the disk cross-sections gives
94	\[
95	\widehat{1_{B_R^3}}(\xi)
96	=\frac{\sin(2\pi Rq)-2\pi Rq\cos(2\pi Rq)}{2\pi^2q^3},
97	\qquad q=\|\xi\|>0.
98	\tag{3.4}
99	\]
100	The triangle inequality gives \(O(Rq^{-2})\) for \(R,q\ge1\), exactly the \(n=3\) case of (3.3).
101	
102	### 3.2 Smoothing and Poisson summation
103	
104	Choose a fixed nonnegative \(C_c^\infty\) function \(\phi\), supported in \(B_1\), with integral one. For example normalize \(\exp[-1/(1-\|x\|^2)]\) inside the unit ball and set it to zero outside. For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), set \(\phi_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\phi(x/\varepsilon)\) and
105	\[
106	f_\pm=1_{B_{R\pm\varepsilon}}*\phi_\varepsilon.
107	\]
108	Pointwise, including the closed-ball boundary,
109	\[
110	f_-\le1_{B_R}\le f_+.
111	\tag{3.5}
112	\]
113	Indeed, an outside point cannot lie within \(\varepsilon\) of \(B_{R-\varepsilon}\); at every point of \(B_R\), the translated support of \(\phi_\varepsilon\) lies in \(B_{R+\varepsilon}\). Nonnegativity and unit integral establish both inequalities.
114	
115	The functions \(f_\pm\) are smooth and compactly supported, hence Schwartz. Poisson summation therefore applies with absolutely convergent Fourier sums:
116	\[
117	\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}f_\pm(z)
118	=V_n(R\pm\varepsilon)^n
119	+\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}
120	\widehat{1_{B_{R\pm\varepsilon}}}(\ell)\widehat\phi(\varepsilon\ell).
121	\tag{3.6}
122	\]
123	For completeness, this instance of Poisson summation follows by periodizing a Schwartz function, computing its Fourier-series coefficients by integration over the unit cube, and evaluating its absolutely convergent Fourier series at zero. It is not being applied directly to a discontinuous ball indicator.
124	
125	For any chosen integer \(M>n\), integration by parts gives
126	\(|\widehat\phi(\eta)|\le C_M(1+\|\eta\|)^{-M}\).
127	Also the number of integer vectors in a unit-width annulus of radius \(j\ge1\) is \(O_n(j^{n-1})\): the disjoint unit cubes centered at those vectors lie in an annulus whose thickness is bounded solely in terms of dimension, and comparison with its volume gives this bound. Thus
128	\[
129	\sum_{\ell\ne0}\|\ell\|^{-(n+1)/2}(1+\varepsilon\|\ell\|)^{-M}
130	\ll_n\sum_{j\ge1}j^{(n-3)/2}(1+\varepsilon j)^{-M}
131	\ll_n\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2}.
132	\tag{3.7}
133	\]
134	To verify the last step, split at \(j=\varepsilon^{-1}\). The lower sum is \(O(\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2})\), since \((n-3)/2>-1\) for \(n\ge2\). For the upper sum, factor out \(\varepsilon^{-M}\) and sum \(j^{(n-3)/2-M}\); it gives the same order. For \(R\ge2\), both \(R\pm\varepsilon\) are comparable to \(R\), so (3.3), (3.5)–(3.7) yield
135	\[
136	|N_0(R)-V_nR^n|
137	\ll_n R^{n-1}\varepsilon
138	+R^{(n-1)/2}\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2}.
139	\tag{3.8}
140	\]
141	The first term here is a **continuous volume difference** \(V_n(R\pm\varepsilon)^n-V_nR^n\). We have not assumed that the discrete count in a thin lattice shell equals its volume; doing that would be an unjustified shortcut.
142	
143	Take \(\varepsilon=R^{-(n-1)/(n+1)}\). The two terms in (3.8) both equal order \(R^{n(n-1)/(n+1)}\), proving (3.1) for every real \(R\ge2\). For \(n=3\), the choices are \(\varepsilon=R^{-1/2}\) and error \(O(R^{3/2})\). ∎
144	
145	## 4. Ranking and ties imply a vanishing radial correction
146	
147	Let \(N(R)=N_0(R)-1\), excluding the origin, and let
148	\(N_<(r)=\#\{z\ne0:\|z\|<r\}\).
149	For a vector on a shell of radius \(r\), every possible rank within the shell satisfies
150	\[
151	N_<(r)+1\le k\le N(r).
152	\tag{4.1}
153	\]
154	Equation (3.1) also gives
155	\[
156	N_<(r)=V_nr^n+O_n(r^{\alpha_n})
157	\tag{4.2}
158	\]
159	For \(r>2\), this follows by letting a real radius \(R\uparrow r\). Counts are locally finite, so that left limit is the strict count. The bound in (3.1) holds uniformly for **all real \(R\ge2\)**, which is essential here. The small shells \(1\le r\le2\) are included directly by increasing the constant: both strict and non-strict counts are at most \(5^n\), the volume term is at most \(V_n2^n\), and \(r^{\alpha_n}\ge1\). This also supplies the needed non-strict count bound below radius two. Subtracting the two estimates bounds the entire tie multiplicity by \(O_n(r^{\alpha_n})\).
160	
161	It follows uniformly for every rank in that shell that
162	\[
163	|k-V_nr^n|\ll_n r^{\alpha_n}.
164	\tag{4.3}
165	\]
166	For \(A=k^{1/n}\), \(B=c_nr\), use
167	\[
168	|A-B|=
169	\frac{|A^n-B^n|}{A^{n-1}+A^{n-2}B+\cdots+B^{n-1}}
170	\le\frac{|k-V_nr^n|}{(c_nr)^{n-1}}.
171	\tag{4.4}
172	\]
173	As \(\alpha_n-(n-1)=-(n-1)/(n+1)\), (4.4) proves (2.2). In particular \(r_k\to\infty\) and the displacement tends to zero uniformly through ties. Lexicographic order is chosen for a reproducible algorithm, not to rescue the estimate.
174	
175	This is exactly the point at which an ordinary leading count asymptotic would be insufficient. For example \((R+1)^n=R^n+O(R^{n-1})\) has the same relative volume main term as \(R^n\), but the associated n-th-root correction equals **one**, not a vanishing quantity. ∎
176	
177	## 5. All-pair separation and global covering
178	
179	Let \(\delta_k=\|s_k-c_nz_k\|\). By (2.2), choose \(K\) such that \(\delta_k\le c_n/4\) for every \(k\ge K\). Distinct integer vectors are at distance at least one. Hence, for distinct \(i,j\ge K\),
180	\[
181	\|s_i-s_j\|\ge c_n\|z_i-z_j\|-\delta_i-\delta_j\ge c_n/2.
182	\tag{5.1}
183	\]
184	This alone does not address the finite initial part. Put \(A=0\) if \(K=1\), and otherwise \(A=(K-1)^{1/n}\). Choose an integer \(L\ge\max(K,2)\) such that \(L^{1/n}>A+1\). If \(i<K\) and \(j\ge L\), the reverse triangle inequality gives
185	\[
186	\|s_j-s_i\|\ge j^{1/n}-i^{1/n}>1.
187	\tag{5.2}
188	\]
189	All remaining pairs have both indices less than \(L\), or are already covered by (5.1). Points with different indices have different norms, so none of these finitely many pairs coincide. More explicitly, since \(x^{1/n}\) is concave,
190	\[
191	\|s_j-s_i\|\ge j^{1/n}-i^{1/n}
192	\ge L^{1/n}-(L-1)^{1/n}>0
193	\quad(1\le i<j<L).
194	\tag{5.3}
195	\]
196	Thus a global separation constant is
197	\[
198	\eta_n=\min\{c_n/2,1,L^{1/n}-(L-1)^{1/n}\}>0.
199	\tag{5.4}
200	\]
201	This proves separation for the entire sequence, including all finite-prefix/cross-prefix pairs. It is not an extrapolation of a sampled minimum distance.
202	
203	Since \(\delta_k\to0\), \(D_n=\sup_k\delta_k<\infty\). For any \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), rounding \(x/c_n\) to an integer vector gives a lattice point at distance at most \(c_n\sqrt n/2\). If that vector is zero, choose \(e_1\) instead, increasing this bound by at most \(c_n\). Every nonzero integer vector occurs in the enumeration, so some \(s_k\) satisfies
204	\[
205	\|x-s_k\|\le c_n(\sqrt n/2+1)+D_n.
206	\tag{5.5}
207	\]
208	Therefore \(S\) is relatively dense. Removing the lattice origin has been explicitly accounted for. ∎
209	
210	## 6. Density for every bounded Jordan-measurable set
211	
212	First, the scaled lattice \(\Lambda=c_n\mathbb Z^n\) has
213	\[
214	\frac{\#(\Lambda\cap RX)}{R^n}\longrightarrow
215	\frac{\lambda_n(X)}{c_n^n}
216	=\frac{\lambda_n(X)}{V_n}
217	\tag{6.1}
218	\]
219	for every bounded Jordan-measurable \(X\). For an axis-aligned box this follows by multiplying the one-dimensional counts \((R/c_n)(b-a)+O(1)\). Finite inner and outer unions of grid boxes, whose volume difference can be made arbitrarily small because \(\lambda_n(\partial X)=0\), prove (6.1) by sandwiching. Removing one point, the origin, changes the count by at most one.
220	
221	We next prove that the bounded displacement \(c_nz_k\mapsto s_k\) preserves this density. Fix \(X\) and \(\epsilon>0\). Its boundary \(\partial X\) is compact and has measure zero, so choose finitely many open axis-aligned boxes whose union \(U\) covers \(\partial X\) and whose **sum of volumes** is less than \(\epsilon\). Compactness gives an \(h>0\) such that the h-neighborhood of \(\partial X\) is contained in \(U\).
222	
223	For sufficiently large \(R\), \(D_n/R<h\). If \(c_nz_k/R\) and \(s_k/R\) differ in membership in \(X\), connectedness of the segment between them gives \(\operatorname{dist}(c_nz_k/R,\partial X)\le\delta_k/R\le D_n/R<h\). Consequently \(c_nz_k/R\in U\). Therefore
224	\[
225	\left|\#(S\cap RX)-\#((\Lambda\setminus\{0\})\cap RX)\right|
226	\le\#(\Lambda\cap RU).
227	\tag{6.2}
228	\]
229	Using the separate box counts, the upper limit of the right side divided by \(R^n\) is at most \(\epsilon/V_n\), even if the covering boxes overlap. Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) proves that the normalized difference tends to zero. Combining with (6.1) proves (2.3).
230	
231	Boundary membership conventions do not affect this argument. No convexity, smoothness, connectedness, or uniform boundary-content bound is required for \(X\). The constants and the chosen box cover may depend on that fixed set, exactly as allowed in the source definition. ∎
232	
233	## 7. Angular uniform distribution and normalization
234	
235	Let \(C\) be a spherical cap, and define its truncated cone
236	\[
237	X_C=\{ru:0<r\le1,\ u\in C\}.
238	\]
239	This is Jordan-measurable: its boundary consists of parts of a sphere, a cone over the boundary of a spherical cap, and the origin, all of n-dimensional measure zero. For the degenerate full/empty caps the conclusion is immediate. Polar coordinates give
240	\[
241	\lambda_n(X_C)=\frac{\sigma_{n-1}(C)}{n}
242	=V_n\frac{\sigma_{n-1}(C)}{\sigma_{n-1}(\mathbb S^{n-1})}.
243	\tag{7.1}
244	\]
245	Since the radii in (2.1) are exact, taking \(R=N^{1/n}\) makes
246	\[
247	\#(S\cap RX_C)=\#\{1\le k\le N:u_k\in C\}.
248	\]
249	Equation (2.4) now follows from (2.3) and (7.1).
250	
251	**Independent count-based check of the same implication.** Apply the lattice Jordan-count argument directly to the cone \(X_C\), at radius \(r_k\). The difference between the first k norm-ordered lattice vectors and the complete ball of radius \(r_k\) is at most the tie multiplicity \(O(r_k^{\alpha_n})=o(r_k^n)\). Dividing the lattice sector count by \(k\sim V_nr_k^n\) gives the same spherical-cap limit, independently of the bounded-displacement density argument.
252	
253	Finally, for the unit ball itself,
254	\[
255	\#(S\cap B_R)=\lfloor R^n\rfloor.
256	\tag{7.2}
257	\]
258	Thus any density \(\rho\) in the source's sense must satisfy \(1=\rho V_n\), i.e. \(\rho=V_n^{-1}\). The rendered pp. 22–23 of the primary source indeed print a **superscript inverse**, not \(V_{n-1}\). The OCR ambiguity is resolved both visually and by this forced normalization. ∎
259	
260	## 8. Effective construction and limits
261	
262	For each integer radius \(M\), enumerate the finite cube \([-M,M]^n\cap\mathbb Z^n\), discard the origin and points whose squared norm exceeds \(M^2\), and sort by the integer key
263	\[
264	(\|z\|_2^2,z_1,\ldots,z_n).
265	\]
266	Increase \(M\) until at least k vectors are present, then take the first k. No point outside that cube has norm at most \(M\); consequently this is exactly the desired initial segment. The process terminates because even the nonzero axis vectors alone increase without bound. Norm comparisons and tie decisions use integers, not rounded square roots. Each direction and each new point is computable to arbitrary precision from integer square roots and positive n-th roots. This is an effectively constructible sequence in the paper's sense; no polynomial-time-in-dimension claim is made.
267	
268	Here “effectively constructible” describes the sequence and its finite prefixes. The proof establishes existence of \(K,L,\eta_n,D_n\), but this package does not compute numerical values of those global Delone constants. In particular the sampled geometric values below are not substitutes for them.
269	
270	
271	The all-dimensional assertion is proved for each fixed \(n\ge2\). The numerical smoke primarily exercises \(n=3\), and does not certify all dimensions by sampling. There is no claimed optimal packing density, best separation constant, minimum energy, or novel Fourier-analytic method. The answer concerns the stated existence problem only. Historical novelty depends on the forward-source screen, not merely on this proof being written here.
272	
273	## 9. Claim ledger and verification/review record

275	| Claim | Evidence category | Novelty status | Load-bearing justification |

277	| Ball discrepancy (3.1) | Reproduction of classical argument / Certification of displayed derivation | Established ingredient, not new | Bessel decay, compact smoothing, absolutely convergent Poisson sum, balanced error terms |

# Norm-ranked lattice spirals: proof and evidence

**Verdict: SOLVED for the exact existence statement below in every fixed dimension \(n\ge2\), hence for every \(n\ge3\) asked about. Correctness state: DELIVERY-READY. Evidence: Certification, not a priority-certified Discovery.** A completed independent other-vendor referee found the proof correct; its minor clarifications and dispositions appear at the end. The broad physics-book cone-energy problem is not solved here.


Date: 2026-10-14 (PT). **Evidence label: Certification of the written theorem below; novelty/priority is not established by this label.** The classical lattice-discrepancy argument is a reproduction of established Fourier/Poisson machinery. Finite computations are Empirical evidence or exact finite identity checks, not a substitute for the infinite-set argument. Independent review and the later-source screen are recorded separately.

## 1. Exact obligation and frozen research contract

The target is the explicit density question in Adiceam–Tsokanos, *Higher Dimensional Spiral Delone Sets*, arXiv:2010.06428v3, §6, pp. 22–23. Their points have **exact radii** \(k^{1/n}\), with arbitrary spherical directions. Their asymptotic-density limit is required for **every bounded measurable set whose boundary has zero Lebesgue measure**. Merely counting origin-centered balls does not answer the question.

- **Claim:** the norm-ranked nonzero integer lattice construction below gives a Delone spiral with the required density and angular uniform distribution in every fixed dimension \(n\ge2\), hence in every dimension asked about, \(n\ge3\).
- **Baseline:** their paper constructs spiral Delone sets in every dimension but explicitly leaves the additional density/angular-equidistribution condition open. The classical smooth-ball lattice discrepancy is an ingredient, not a claimed new estimate.
- **Load-bearing bridge:** an error \(o(R^{n-1})\) in the lattice-ball count makes the radial rank correction \(o(1)\), including all points tied on a lattice sphere. A volume main term \(N(R)\sim V_nR^n\) alone does not supply that bridge.
- **Scope:** arbitrary directions are allowed by the source definition. No continuity, bounded step between consecutive indices, transitive-map orbit, distinctness of directions, or visually sunflower-like appearance is claimed. The points themselves are distinct because their radii are distinct. Every nonzero lattice vector is used, including nonprimitive vectors.
- **Book connection:** this is a higher-dimensional phyllotaxis/regular-packing subproblem, not a theorem about elastic energy, cone packing, Fibonacci optimality, or a minimum-energy configuration.
- **Frozen scientific controls:** two independent exact lattice enumerators, complete and partially cut tie shells, normalization and exponent identities, 3D ball Fourier-transform identity, and deterministic 3D geometric/density observations. Main geometric sample: all nonzero integer points in the ball of radius 24; smaller radii 4, 8, 12, 16 check prefix consistency. Directional counts and translated Jordan-box counts include negative controls. No optimizer, fitted parameter, or learned model is used. Single-thread numerical libraries; no giant search.

## 2. The theorem

Write
\[
V_n=\lambda_n(B_1)=\frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(1+n/2)},\qquad c_n=V_n^{1/n}.
\]
Enumerate \(\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) as \((z_k)_{k\ge1}\), in nondecreasing Euclidean norm, with lexicographic order within equal-norm shells. Put
\[
r_k=\|z_k\|_2,\qquad u_k=z_k/r_k,\qquad s_k=k^{1/n}u_k,\qquad S=\{s_k:k\ge1\}.
\tag{2.1}
\]

**Theorem.** For each fixed integer \(n\ge2\):

1. (2.1) is effectively constructible and \(\|s_k\|_2=k^{1/n}\) exactly.
2. With \(\beta_n=(n-1)/(n+1)>0\),
   \[
   \|s_k-c_nz_k\|_2=O_n(r_k^{-\beta_n})=o(1).
   \tag{2.2}
   \]
   The estimate is uniform over all ranks within any tied shell; the conclusion does not depend on the chosen order inside ties.
3. \(S\) is uniformly discrete and relatively dense in \(\mathbb R^n\), including the finite initial part.
4. For every bounded Jordan-measurable \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\),
   \[
   \lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{\#(S\cap RX)}{R^n}
   =\frac{\lambda_n(X)}{V_n}.
   \tag{2.3}
   \]
5. For every spherical cap \(C\subset\mathbb S^{n-1}\),
   \[
   \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\#\{1\le k\le N:u_k\in C\}}{N}
   =\frac{\sigma_{n-1}(C)}{\sigma_{n-1}(\mathbb S^{n-1})}.
   \tag{2.4}
   \]

No numerical value of the global separation or covering constant is inferred from a finite nearest-neighbor computation. Their existence is proved in §5.

## 3. Ball-count lemma, with a special-case proof

Define the full closed-ball count
\[
N_0(R)=\#\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:\|z\|_2\le R\}.
\]
For all real \(R\ge2\), we prove
\[
N_0(R)=V_nR^n+O_n(R^{\alpha_n}),\qquad
\alpha_n=\frac{n(n-1)}{n+1}=n-2+\frac{2}{n+1}.
\tag{3.1}
\]
In particular \(\alpha_n<n-1\). The constant may depend on fixed dimension; no dimension-uniform constant is asserted.

### 3.1 Fourier transform and its decay

Use the Fourier convention
\(\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx\).
For \(\xi\ne0\), rotation invariance and slicing perpendicular to \(\xi\) give
\[
\widehat{1_{B_R}}(\xi)
=V_{n-1}\int_{-R}^{R}(R^2-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}
 e^{-2\pi i\|\xi\|t}\,dt
=R^{n/2}\|\xi\|^{-n/2}J_{n/2}(2\pi R\|\xi\|).
\tag{3.2}
\]
The last equality is Poisson's Bessel integral, [NIST DLMF 10.9.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.9.E4), with fixed real order \(\nu=n/2>-1/2\). The constants follow from \(V_{n-1}=\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)\); substituting \(t=Rv\) into the first integral makes (3.2) immediate from that identity.

For fixed order, [DLMF 10.17.3](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.17.E3) gives
\(J_{n/2}(x)=O_n(x^{-1/2})\) as positive real \(x\to\infty\). Continuity on compact positive intervals extends the bound to all \(x\ge1\). Hence, when \(R\ge1\) and \(\|\xi\|\ge1\),
\[
|\widehat{1_{B_R}}(\xi)|
\le A_n R^{(n-1)/2}\|\xi\|^{-(n+1)/2}.
\tag{3.3}
\]
These are established special-function identities; neither the formula nor its decay is a new result here.

For the requested ambient dimension three, no Bessel asymptotic is necessary: direct integration of the disk cross-sections gives
\[
\widehat{1_{B_R^3}}(\xi)
=\frac{\sin(2\pi Rq)-2\pi Rq\cos(2\pi Rq)}{2\pi^2q^3},
\qquad q=\|\xi\|>0.
\tag{3.4}
\]
The triangle inequality gives \(O(Rq^{-2})\) for \(R,q\ge1\), exactly the \(n=3\) case of (3.3).

### 3.2 Smoothing and Poisson summation

Choose a fixed nonnegative \(C_c^\infty\) function \(\phi\), supported in \(B_1\), with integral one. For example normalize \(\exp[-1/(1-\|x\|^2)]\) inside the unit ball and set it to zero outside. For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), set \(\phi_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\phi(x/\varepsilon)\) and
\[
f_\pm=1_{B_{R\pm\varepsilon}}*\phi_\varepsilon.
\]
Pointwise, including the closed-ball boundary,
\[
f_-\le1_{B_R}\le f_+.
\tag{3.5}
\]
Indeed, an outside point cannot lie within \(\varepsilon\) of \(B_{R-\varepsilon}\); at every point of \(B_R\), the translated support of \(\phi_\varepsilon\) lies in \(B_{R+\varepsilon}\). Nonnegativity and unit integral establish both inequalities.

The functions \(f_\pm\) are smooth and compactly supported, hence Schwartz. Poisson summation therefore applies with absolutely convergent Fourier sums:
\[
\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}f_\pm(z)
=V_n(R\pm\varepsilon)^n
+\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}
\widehat{1_{B_{R\pm\varepsilon}}}(\ell)\widehat\phi(\varepsilon\ell).
\tag{3.6}
\]
For completeness, this instance of Poisson summation follows by periodizing a Schwartz function, computing its Fourier-series coefficients by integration over the unit cube, and evaluating its absolutely convergent Fourier series at zero. It is not being applied directly to a discontinuous ball indicator.

For any chosen integer \(M>n\), integration by parts gives
\(|\widehat\phi(\eta)|\le C_M(1+\|\eta\|)^{-M}\).
Also the number of integer vectors in a unit-width annulus of radius \(j\ge1\) is \(O_n(j^{n-1})\): the disjoint unit cubes centered at those vectors lie in an annulus whose thickness is bounded solely in terms of dimension, and comparison with its volume gives this bound. Thus
\[
\sum_{\ell\ne0}\|\ell\|^{-(n+1)/2}(1+\varepsilon\|\ell\|)^{-M}
\ll_n\sum_{j\ge1}j^{(n-3)/2}(1+\varepsilon j)^{-M}
\ll_n\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2}.
\tag{3.7}
\]
To verify the last step, split at \(j=\varepsilon^{-1}\). The lower sum is \(O(\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2})\), since \((n-3)/2>-1\) for \(n\ge2\). For the upper sum, factor out \(\varepsilon^{-M}\) and sum \(j^{(n-3)/2-M}\); it gives the same order. For \(R\ge2\), both \(R\pm\varepsilon\) are comparable to \(R\), so (3.3), (3.5)–(3.7) yield
\[
|N_0(R)-V_nR^n|
\ll_n R^{n-1}\varepsilon
+R^{(n-1)/2}\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2}.
\tag{3.8}
\]
The first term here is a **continuous volume difference** \(V_n(R\pm\varepsilon)^n-V_nR^n\). We have not assumed that the discrete count in a thin lattice shell equals its volume; doing that would be an unjustified shortcut.

Take \(\varepsilon=R^{-(n-1)/(n+1)}\). The two terms in (3.8) both equal order \(R^{n(n-1)/(n+1)}\), proving (3.1) for every real \(R\ge2\). For \(n=3\), the choices are \(\varepsilon=R^{-1/2}\) and error \(O(R^{3/2})\). ∎

## 4. Ranking and ties imply a vanishing radial correction

Let \(N(R)=N_0(R)-1\), excluding the origin, and let
\(N_<(r)=\#\{z\ne0:\|z\|<r\}\).
For a vector on a shell of radius \(r\), every possible rank within the shell satisfies
\[
N_<(r)+1\le k\le N(r).
\tag{4.1}
\]
Equation (3.1) also gives
\[
N_<(r)=V_nr^n+O_n(r^{\alpha_n})
\tag{4.2}
\]
For \(r>2\), this follows by letting a real radius \(R\uparrow r\). Counts are locally finite, so that left limit is the strict count. The bound in (3.1) holds uniformly for **all real \(R\ge2\)**, which is essential here. The small shells \(1\le r\le2\) are included directly by increasing the constant: both strict and non-strict counts are at most \(5^n\), the volume term is at most \(V_n2^n\), and \(r^{\alpha_n}\ge1\). This also supplies the needed non-strict count bound below radius two. Subtracting the two estimates bounds the entire tie multiplicity by \(O_n(r^{\alpha_n})\).

It follows uniformly for every rank in that shell that
\[
|k-V_nr^n|\ll_n r^{\alpha_n}.
\tag{4.3}
\]
For \(A=k^{1/n}\), \(B=c_nr\), use
\[
|A-B|=
\frac{|A^n-B^n|}{A^{n-1}+A^{n-2}B+\cdots+B^{n-1}}
\le\frac{|k-V_nr^n|}{(c_nr)^{n-1}}.
\tag{4.4}
\]
As \(\alpha_n-(n-1)=-(n-1)/(n+1)\), (4.4) proves (2.2). In particular \(r_k\to\infty\) and the displacement tends to zero uniformly through ties. Lexicographic order is chosen for a reproducible algorithm, not to rescue the estimate.

This is exactly the point at which an ordinary leading count asymptotic would be insufficient. For example \((R+1)^n=R^n+O(R^{n-1})\) has the same relative volume main term as \(R^n\), but the associated n-th-root correction equals **one**, not a vanishing quantity. ∎

## 5. All-pair separation and global covering

Let \(\delta_k=\|s_k-c_nz_k\|\). By (2.2), choose \(K\) such that \(\delta_k\le c_n/4\) for every \(k\ge K\). Distinct integer vectors are at distance at least one. Hence, for distinct \(i,j\ge K\),
\[
\|s_i-s_j\|\ge c_n\|z_i-z_j\|-\delta_i-\delta_j\ge c_n/2.
\tag{5.1}
\]
This alone does not address the finite initial part. Put \(A=0\) if \(K=1\), and otherwise \(A=(K-1)^{1/n}\). Choose an integer \(L\ge\max(K,2)\) such that \(L^{1/n}>A+1\). If \(i<K\) and \(j\ge L\), the reverse triangle inequality gives
\[
\|s_j-s_i\|\ge j^{1/n}-i^{1/n}>1.
\tag{5.2}
\]
All remaining pairs have both indices less than \(L\), or are already covered by (5.1). Points with different indices have different norms, so none of these finitely many pairs coincide. More explicitly, since \(x^{1/n}\) is concave,
\[
\|s_j-s_i\|\ge j^{1/n}-i^{1/n}
\ge L^{1/n}-(L-1)^{1/n}>0
\quad(1\le i<j<L).
\tag{5.3}
\]
Thus a global separation constant is
\[
\eta_n=\min\{c_n/2,1,L^{1/n}-(L-1)^{1/n}\}>0.
\tag{5.4}
\]
This proves separation for the entire sequence, including all finite-prefix/cross-prefix pairs. It is not an extrapolation of a sampled minimum distance.

Since \(\delta_k\to0\), \(D_n=\sup_k\delta_k<\infty\). For any \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), rounding \(x/c_n\) to an integer vector gives a lattice point at distance at most \(c_n\sqrt n/2\). If that vector is zero, choose \(e_1\) instead, increasing this bound by at most \(c_n\). Every nonzero integer vector occurs in the enumeration, so some \(s_k\) satisfies
\[
\|x-s_k\|\le c_n(\sqrt n/2+1)+D_n.
\tag{5.5}
\]
Therefore \(S\) is relatively dense. Removing the lattice origin has been explicitly accounted for. ∎

## 6. Density for every bounded Jordan-measurable set

First, the scaled lattice \(\Lambda=c_n\mathbb Z^n\) has
\[
\frac{\#(\Lambda\cap RX)}{R^n}\longrightarrow
\frac{\lambda_n(X)}{c_n^n}
=\frac{\lambda_n(X)}{V_n}
\tag{6.1}
\]
for every bounded Jordan-measurable \(X\). For an axis-aligned box this follows by multiplying the one-dimensional counts \((R/c_n)(b-a)+O(1)\). Finite inner and outer unions of grid boxes, whose volume difference can be made arbitrarily small because \(\lambda_n(\partial X)=0\), prove (6.1) by sandwiching. Removing one point, the origin, changes the count by at most one.

We next prove that the bounded displacement \(c_nz_k\mapsto s_k\) preserves this density. Fix \(X\) and \(\epsilon>0\). Its boundary \(\partial X\) is compact and has measure zero, so choose finitely many open axis-aligned boxes whose union \(U\) covers \(\partial X\) and whose **sum of volumes** is less than \(\epsilon\). Compactness gives an \(h>0\) such that the h-neighborhood of \(\partial X\) is contained in \(U\).

For sufficiently large \(R\), \(D_n/R<h\). If \(c_nz_k/R\) and \(s_k/R\) differ in membership in \(X\), connectedness of the segment between them gives \(\operatorname{dist}(c_nz_k/R,\partial X)\le\delta_k/R\le D_n/R<h\). Consequently \(c_nz_k/R\in U\). Therefore
\[
\left|\#(S\cap RX)-\#((\Lambda\setminus\{0\})\cap RX)\right|
\le\#(\Lambda\cap RU).
\tag{6.2}
\]
Using the separate box counts, the upper limit of the right side divided by \(R^n\) is at most \(\epsilon/V_n\), even if the covering boxes overlap. Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) proves that the normalized difference tends to zero. Combining with (6.1) proves (2.3).

Boundary membership conventions do not affect this argument. No convexity, smoothness, connectedness, or uniform boundary-content bound is required for \(X\). The constants and the chosen box cover may depend on that fixed set, exactly as allowed in the source definition. ∎

## 7. Angular uniform distribution and normalization

Let \(C\) be a spherical cap, and define its truncated cone
\[
X_C=\{ru:0<r\le1,\ u\in C\}.
\]
This is Jordan-measurable: its boundary consists of parts of a sphere, a cone over the boundary of a spherical cap, and the origin, all of n-dimensional measure zero. For the degenerate full/empty caps the conclusion is immediate. Polar coordinates give
\[
\lambda_n(X_C)=\frac{\sigma_{n-1}(C)}{n}
=V_n\frac{\sigma_{n-1}(C)}{\sigma_{n-1}(\mathbb S^{n-1})}.
\tag{7.1}
\]
Since the radii in (2.1) are exact, taking \(R=N^{1/n}\) makes
\[
\#(S\cap RX_C)=\#\{1\le k\le N:u_k\in C\}.
\]
Equation (2.4) now follows from (2.3) and (7.1).

**Independent count-based check of the same implication.** Apply the lattice Jordan-count argument directly to the cone \(X_C\), at radius \(r_k\). The difference between the first k norm-ordered lattice vectors and the complete ball of radius \(r_k\) is at most the tie multiplicity \(O(r_k^{\alpha_n})=o(r_k^n)\). Dividing the lattice sector count by \(k\sim V_nr_k^n\) gives the same spherical-cap limit, independently of the bounded-displacement density argument.

Finally, for the unit ball itself,
\[
\#(S\cap B_R)=\lfloor R^n\rfloor.
\tag{7.2}
\]
Thus any density \(\rho\) in the source's sense must satisfy \(1=\rho V_n\), i.e. \(\rho=V_n^{-1}\). The rendered pp. 22–23 of the primary source indeed print a **superscript inverse**, not \(V_{n-1}\). The OCR ambiguity is resolved both visually and by this forced normalization. ∎

## 8. Effective construction and limits

For each integer radius \(M\), enumerate the finite cube \([-M,M]^n\cap\mathbb Z^n\), discard the origin and points whose squared norm exceeds \(M^2\), and sort by the integer key
\[
(\|z\|_2^2,z_1,\ldots,z_n).
\]
Increase \(M\) until at least k vectors are present, then take the first k. No point outside that cube has norm at most \(M\); consequently this is exactly the desired initial segment. The process terminates because even the nonzero axis vectors alone increase without bound. Norm comparisons and tie decisions use integers, not rounded square roots. Each direction and each new point is computable to arbitrary precision from integer square roots and positive n-th roots. This is an effectively constructible sequence in the paper's sense; no polynomial-time-in-dimension claim is made.

Here “effectively constructible” describes the sequence and its finite prefixes. The proof establishes existence of \(K,L,\eta_n,D_n\), but this package does not compute numerical values of those global Delone constants. In particular the sampled geometric values below are not substitutes for them.


The all-dimensional assertion is proved for each fixed \(n\ge2\). The numerical smoke primarily exercises \(n=3\), and does not certify all dimensions by sampling. There is no claimed optimal packing density, best separation constant, minimum energy, or novel Fourier-analytic method. The answer concerns the stated existence problem only. Historical novelty depends on the forward-source screen, not merely on this proof being written here.

| Ball discrepancy (3.1) | Reproduction of classical argument / Certification of displayed derivation | Established ingredient, not new | Bessel decay, compact smoothing, absolutely convergent Poisson sum, balanced error terms |

The topology uses **translations only**, with translation vectors escaping to infinity. Nonempty limits are affine translates, not necessarily groups through zero.

In particular neither the plane nor a translate of `R x Z` occurs. For each irrational non-BA alpha, establish that line and lattice types actually occur, with empty limits handled separately.

Bacher's 2014 Theorem 1.1 already gives uniform local lattice approximation; its Remark 3.3 gives the exact area pi. 41	The relevant statements in the **refereed PDF**, whose numbering differs from arXiv:1301.7568, are:
42	
43	- **Theorem 1.1:** uniform-in-angle local approximation near distant spiral points by affine lattices, with an explicitly identified similarity class. Its definition of epsilon-closeness covers both local directions.
44	- **Proposition 3.1 and Corollary 3.2:** the actual continued-fraction-basis linearization, with local error of order `1/sqrt(n)`.
45	- **Remark 3.3:** the linearized lattice has fundamental area **pi** exactly. Our lattice `L_n={(q/(2sqrt(n)),2*pi*sqrt(n)*(q*alpha-p))}` is the same object after a unimodular integer basis change.

Read with his one-to-one local description, it already asserts the affirmative lattice-limit covolume answer in Voronoi-area form: with nonmerging local convergence, the Voronoi cells converge to the lattice cell. This implication is our reading of his statements, not a named Chabauty theorem in his paper. 47	- **Proposition 6.1:** states equivalence of bounded continued-fraction coefficients with uniform discreteness/relative density and compactness of the shape orbit, then says the proof is left to the reader. For the optional BA no-empty boundary, our actual proof source is the inspected Akiyama Theorem 2 below.
48	
49	**Material overlap:** combining Bacher's uniform local description and area normalization with the elementary fixed-covolume planar-lattice compactification already gives the classification route. Our contribution is a self-contained quantitative certification and explicit application to the question posed in 2025, with both local inclusions, affine recentering, type realizability and negative controls written out. It is **not** a new local-lattice mechanism. A first-priority claim would require a broader review of earlier consequences and literature; none is made here.

Nevertheless, the implication from his results is transparent and should be acknowledged as a **classical corollary**, not hidden to manufacture originality. Tevet's inspected references do not cite Bacher. An explicit later conjecture does not erase earlier mathematical ingredients or their consequences.
52	
53	### Additional direct baselines requested by the referee
54	
55	**Y. Yamagishi, T. Sushida and J.-F. Sadoc**, *Area convergence of Voronoi cells on spiral lattices*, **Nonlinearity 34** (2021), 3163–3183, DOI [10.1088/1361-6544/abe733](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6544/abe733); primary [arXiv:2006.14723v1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.14723v1), Theorem 1 and Corollary 2, p. 2, now read and pinned. **Both explicitly assume the angle divided by 2*pi is badly approximable.** With radial exponent 1/2 their conclusion is area pi. The unversioned arXiv landing page identifies v1 as its only version; a secondary search listing suggesting another revision was not adopted.

This is a proved source for the boundary fact Bacher had announced without proof. It does not classify nonempty non-BA Chabauty limits.

82	2. classify limits of fixed-covolume planar lattices by a shortest vector and a reduced complementary vector;

109	**Reduced-basis fact.** For any such lattice choose a shortest nonzero vector u and write `ell=|u|`.
